newsitem.title: FRANCE: Key unions pledge battle on French rail reform.
newsitem.headline: Key unions pledge battle on French rail reform.

text.p: The French government launches its rescue plan for the SNCF state railways through the Senate on Tuesday with two key unions vowing a bruising battle as labour unrest looms in several other sectors.

Train drivers in the CFDT union, France's biggest, have appealed for a nationwide rail strike on January 31 in protest at the overhaul which is part of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's reform drive. Unions say it could lead to job losses.
Unions in a host of other sectors, encouraged by government concessions won by truckers after a crippling 12-day strike in November, have been scrambling to jump on the bandwaggon.

In Paris, Credit Foncier bank officials were held hostage by employees for a fourth day on Monday in a standoff with the government over job security and the bank's fate. Urban transport workers outside Paris plan a stoppage on Friday.

"I can tell you that in late February there will be an announcement that thousands of jobs have been scrapped," Bernard Thibault, head of the rail branch of the Communist CGT union, told Europe-1 radio.

Asked whether the CGT would also stage a strike, he said: "That's going to be decided in the next few days. We're convinced the plan does not correspond to the government's commitments, it jeopardises the rail network and jobs."

Memories are still vivid in France of a late 1995 strike by railway and other public transport workers which paralysed the country for more than three weeks just ahead of the Christmas holiday season.

"Things are going to be a bit bumpy," said one Juppe aide of the labour turbulence partly prompted by the premier yielding to truckers' demands for early retirement, shorter working hours and higher pay.
Six of eight trade unions are ready to back the SNCF reform which would create a state company to take over 134.2 billion francs ($24.87 billion) of SNCF debts totalling 208 billion.

SNCF chairman Louis Gallois, in an interview with the daily Le Parisien, said the overhaul would benefit travellers who in some cases would see cheaper fares, and pledged that rail staff would not lose their benefits.
"Without the reform, the SNCF would be asphyxiated...We're going to try to provide a better service at a lower cost," Gallois said.
"I won't make any forecasts on possible strikes...Railway workers are more ready for reform than commonly-believed. They don't want the negative image that people often have of them," Gallois added.
Transport Minister Bernard Pons said last week there was no question of delaying reform of the SNCF, already put on hold in November as he sought to appease unions, in the face of the strike call.

The new state company, likely to be called France Rail, would become owner of the infrastructure and charge the SNCF, which would continue as railways operator and maintain the infrastructure, fees for use of Europe's biggest rail network.

The Socialist CFDT and Communist-led CGT unions argue that the split amounts to a break-up and a precursor to opening France's railways to competition. But they have not yet hit on a common strategy to combat it.
